answer.question: Which patients are eligible for the hybrid hospital-wide readmission measure?
answer.answer: Eligible patients are Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries aged 65 or older, with Part A enrollment for the 12 months through the index admission, discharged alive from a non-federal acute-care hospital. Patients younger than 65 and Medicare Advantage enrollees are not included. Transfers are included in the measure, but the readmission outcome is attributed to the hospital that ultimately discharges the patient to a non-acute-care setting. The measure excludes admissions to PPS-exempt cancer hospitals; patients without at least 30 days of post-discharge FFS Medicare enrollment; discharges against medical advice; and admissions for primary psychiatric diagnoses, rehabilitation, or medical cancer treatment. Patients admitted for other diagnoses or for surgical cancer treatment remain eligible.

answer.question: What changed when Medicare Advantage admissions were added to the hospital-wide readmission measure?
answer.answer: The only specification change was adding Medicare Advantage (MA) admissions to the cohort; all other measure specifications stayed the same. In the July 1, 2018–June 30, 2019 test, this added 127 hospitals and more than four million admissions; among hospitals meeting the 25-admission public-reporting cutoff, 63 additional hospitals were included. The combined FFS-and-MA group had a mean risk-standardized readmission rate of 15.48%, compared with 15.35% for FFS-only, and higher test-retest reliability (0.780 versus 0.725). About 67% of hospitals stayed in the same performance quintile and 95% stayed within one quintile; the largest shifts were at hospitals with a high share of MA admissions. Adding MA admissions improved reliability and score precision and included more hospitals and beneficiaries. Testing used the claims-only measure because EHR data were unavailable; the report expected the impact to be comparable for the hybrid measure.

answer.question: How does the hybrid hospital-wide mortality measure account for different mixes of services across hospitals?
answer.answer: The measure groups admissions into 15 mutually exclusive service-line divisions based on discharge diagnoses or procedures, and adjusts for service mix using the principal discharge-diagnosis category. It calculates a separate standardized mortality ratio for each division at each hospital, then combines the division results in a volume-weighted average that also accounts for how precisely each division’s outcome was predicted. answer.question: How are the 1-to-5 star ratings assigned to each individual HCAHPS measure?
answer.answer: For each of the 10 publicly reported HCAHPS measures, CMS first calculates a hospital-level linear score from survey responses. Scores are adjusted for patient mix and survey mode, combined across four quarters using weights based on eligible patients, and rounded to an integer. CMS then assigns 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 whole stars using a clustering method that groups similar measure scores, with boundaries based on gaps in their distribution. The method aims to minimize score variation within each group and distinguish scores between groups; it does not assign partial stars.

answer.answer: SEP-1 calculates the proportion of Medicare beneficiaries with severe sepsis or septic shock who received all applicable elements of the management bundle. records.question: Which interventions make up the SEP-1 numerator, and which patients are excluded?

answer.question: Which interventions make up the SEP-1 numerator, and which patients are excluded?
answer.answer: The numerator includes patients who received all applicable interventions: initial lactate measurement, blood cultures, antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, repeat lactate measurement, vasopressors, and reassessment of volume status and tissue perfusion. For severe sepsis, initial lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, and antibiotics are required within three hours of presentation; repeat lactate is required within six hours if the initial lactate is greater than 2 mmol/L. For septic shock, 30 ml/kg crystalloid is required within three hours for hypotension or lactate = 4 mmol/L; within six hours, vasopressors are required for hypotension unresponsive to initial fluids, and reassessment is required for persistent hypotension (MAP < 65 mm Hg) after fluids or initial lactate = 4 mmol/L. Excluded patients include those without severe sepsis; transferred from another acute care facility; receiving intravenous antibiotics for more than 24 hours before severe sepsis presentation; with a comfort or palliative-care directive within three hours of severe sepsis presentation or within six hours of septic-shock presentation; with an administrative contraindication to care within six hours of severe-sepsis or septic-shock presentation; discharged within six hours of presentation with severe sepsis or septic shock; with a length of stay longer than 120 days; or included in a clinical trial.
